quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE SITUATION
quests.situation: It is seven o'clock on a weekday morning. Describe what you do at home before you leave for work or school.
quests.hint: Say what you do in the order it happens, with one action in each sentence.
quests.explanation: Present simple verbs such as get up, eat and leave are the natural way to describe a routine. Starting most sentences with I keeps the writer clear and the actions easy to follow.
quests.modelAnswer: My alarm rings at seven, so I get up and brush my teeth. I eat cereal with milk in the kitchen. Then I take my bag and leave.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS
quests.situation: The English lesson is about to start. Describe what the teacher and the students do in the classroom.
quests.hint: Give the teacher one or two actions and the students one or two actions.
quests.explanation: A description of a scene names who is present and gives each person a clear verb. Using the teacher and the students as separate subjects shows the reader who does what.
quests.modelAnswer: The teacher comes in and says good morning. The students sit at their desks and open their books. Then the teacher writes a new word on the board.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT YOU SEE
quests.situation: You stand at your apartment window on Saturday morning and look down at the street. Describe what you can see.
quests.hint: Picture the street and name three different things, then say what is happening near each one.
quests.explanation: The phrase I can see introduces what is visible, and a present verb then shows the movement. Mixing places, people and objects gives a fuller picture than a list of things alone.
quests.modelAnswer: I can see a small bakery across the street, and it is already open. A man walks his dog under the trees while two children ride their bikes on the sidewalk.

quests.instruction: WRITE A CLEAR DESCRIPTION
quests.situation: You go to the grocery store after work to buy food for dinner. Describe what you buy and what you do at the checkout.
quests.hint: Name the actual things you buy, and finish with what you do when you are ready to pay.
quests.explanation: Specific nouns like carrots and rice give the reader real information, while some things gives none. Choosing exact words is the quickest way to make a short description useful.
quests.modelAnswer: After work I go to the grocery store and take a basket. I buy carrots, bread, and rice for dinner. At the checkout, I pay the cashier and carry the bags home.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PEOPLE AND WHAT THEY DO
quests.situation: It is Sunday afternoon and your family is together at home. Describe who is there and what each person is doing.
quests.hint: Choose three family members and give each one a different action, so the room feels busy.
quests.explanation: When a scene has several people, use a different subject in each sentence with present continuous. That way the reader sees the whole room instead of one person.
quests.modelAnswer: My grandmother is watching TV in the living room. My father is cooking soup in the kitchen, and my little brother is playing a game on the floor.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PLACE AND WHAT HAPPENS
quests.situation: You wait at a bus stop on a rainy morning with other people. Describe the place, the people, and what happens when the bus comes.
quests.hint: Start with where you are and who is waiting, then move to the moment the bus arrives.
quests.explanation: Setting the scene first and then moving to an event gives a description a natural shape. A word like when links the waiting to the arrival so the reader can follow the change.
quests.modelAnswer: Five people wait at the bus stop, and it is raining hard. A woman holds a big umbrella, and a boy sits on the bench. When the bus arrives, everyone gets on quickly.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS IN ORDER
quests.situation: You arrive at your office on Monday morning. Describe what you do during your first ten minutes at work.
quests.hint: Put your actions in the order they happen and use a word like then or after that once or twice.
quests.explanation: Time connectors such as then and after that turn a list of actions into a sequence. Use them where the order matters, not in every sentence.
quests.modelAnswer: I arrive at the office at nine and say hello to my coworkers. Then I turn on my computer and make a cup of coffee. After that, I check my calendar for meetings.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT YOU DO BEFORE THE DOORBELL RINGS
quests.situation: A friend is coming to your apartment for dinner at seven. Describe how you get ready before the doorbell rings.
quests.hint: Think about what must be finished before your guest can come in, and put those jobs in a sensible order.
quests.explanation: Preparation is easier to follow when each job comes before the one that depends on it. Ending with the moment the guest arrives closes the description neatly.
quests.modelAnswer: First I tidy the living room and set the table for two. Then I cook pasta and make a simple sauce. At seven o'clock the doorbell rings, and I go to open the door.

quests.instruction: USE THE CLUES TO DESCRIBE THE SITUATION
quests.situation: You are at a train station and need to travel to another city. Describe how you buy a ticket and find the right train.
quests.hint: Decide which step comes first, and mention how you know which train and platform are the right ones.
quests.explanation: In a simple process, each step should answer the question what next. Adding where the information comes from, like a sign or a screen, makes the description more realistic than a bare list of actions.
quests.modelAnswer: I go to the ticket machine and buy a ticket to the city. Then I look at the screen to find my train. It leaves from platform four, so I walk there and wait.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PLACE AND THE ACTIONS
quests.situation: It is lunch time in the school cafeteria. Describe the room and what the students are doing.
quests.hint: Begin with how the room feels, then show two groups of students doing different things.
quests.explanation: One general sentence about the whole place, followed by specific actions, is a useful pattern for busy scenes. The general sentence sets the picture and the details prove it.
quests.modelAnswer: The cafeteria is full and very noisy. Some students are eating sandwiches at the long tables, and others are standing in line for hot food. Everyone is talking and laughing.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PEOPLE, ACTIONS, AND RESULT
quests.situation: Your neighbor knocks on your door and asks for help with something. Describe who comes, what he or she asks, and what you do.
quests.hint: Say what the neighbor wants and what you decide, then add how the moment ends.
quests.explanation: Asking and answering are the core of many everyday scenes. Reporting a request with asks to borrow, and then giving your response, shows both sides of the exchange.
quests.modelAnswer: My neighbor knocks on my door and asks to borrow a ladder. I bring it from the storage room and give it to him. He says thank you and promises to return it tonight.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT DIFFERENT PEOPLE ARE DOING
quests.situation: You sit on a bench in a city park on a sunny Sunday. Describe what different people are doing around you.
quests.hint: Notice at least three groups of people and give each group its own activity.
quests.explanation: Present continuous is the tense for actions in progress at the moment you describe. Choosing a different activity for each group means every sentence adds new information.
quests.modelAnswer: A family is having a picnic on a blanket near the trees. Some teenagers are playing football on the grass, and an old man is reading a newspaper on the next bench.

quests.instruction: TAP THE EMOJIS AND DESCRIBE THE SITUATION
quests.situation: You and a friend go to a small café for lunch. Describe what you order and what you do while you wait for the food.
quests.hint: Say what you choose first, then what you and your friend do until the food comes.
quests.explanation: Linking words such as while let you show two things happening together. Here the waiting time becomes a second action instead of a gap in the description.
quests.modelAnswer: We sit by the window, and the waiter gives us the menu. I order a chicken sandwich, and my friend chooses pasta. While we wait, we drink coffee and talk about our weekend.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS FROM START TO FINISH
quests.situation: Your manager gives you a new task on Tuesday morning. Describe what she says and what you do after the conversation.
quests.hint: Report the request first, then show how you organize yourself to complete it.
quests.explanation: After says or asks, you can report what another person wants: she asks me to send a report. Following it with your own actions shows both the instruction and your response.
quests.modelAnswer: My manager asks me to send a report to a client by Friday. After the meeting, I write a list of the steps I need to follow. Then I start the first part on my computer.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PEOPLE AND WHERE THEY GO
quests.situation: Your family arrives at the airport early in the morning for a holiday trip. Describe what you carry and where you go first.
quests.hint: Mention what each person carries and give the order of the first two places you go to.
quests.explanation: Concrete detail such as who carries what makes a travel scene believable. Using first or then once, at the right moment, is enough to show the route.
quests.modelAnswer: We arrive at the airport at six in the morning. My father pushes a cart with three suitcases, and I carry my backpack. First we go to the check-in desk, and then we walk to security.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS AND WHAT YOU DO
quests.situation: You are reading in the living room when it suddenly starts to rain. Your clothes are outside on the balcony. Describe what you do.
quests.hint: Start with what you are doing, then show the sudden change and your quick reaction.
quests.explanation: A short when clause can introduce a sudden change: when it starts to rain, I run outside. The reaction that follows shows the reader why the change matters.
quests.modelAnswer: I am reading a book when it starts to rain. My clothes are still on the balcony, so I run outside, take them in, and close the door behind me.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE CONVERSATION AND THE RESULT
quests.situation: You go to a pharmacy because you have a headache. Describe how you talk to the pharmacist and what you buy.
quests.hint: Include what you say, how the pharmacist answers, and what you buy at the end.
quests.explanation: Describing a short conversation means giving both sides: what one person asks and how the other replies. Verbs like ask, answer and recommend tell the reader who speaks without needing exact quotes.
quests.modelAnswer: I have a headache, so I go to the pharmacy near my house. I ask the pharmacist for something simple, and she recommends a small box of tablets. I pay at the counter and go home.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PLACE, THE PEOPLE, AND ONE ACTION
quests.situation: There is a small street market in your neighborhood on Saturday morning. Describe the stalls, the people, and something you buy.
quests.hint: Choose one stall to describe in detail, then say what you buy there.
quests.explanation: Zooming in on one stall gives a description a clear focus. Details such as prices, quantities or a short exchange with the seller show what makes the market real.
quests.modelAnswer: On Saturday mornings, our street market has many colorful stalls. A farmer sells fresh tomatoes and cheap eggs, and the street is full of people. I chat with him and buy a kilo of tomatoes.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS AND WHY
quests.situation: You arrive late for class this morning. Describe why you are late and what happens when you come into the room.
quests.hint: Give the reason for being late in one sentence, then show how you and the teacher react.
quests.explanation: The word because gives the reason for an event inside the same sentence. Stating the reason first lets the reader understand the situation before seeing your reaction to it.
quests.modelAnswer: I am late for class because my bus comes ten minutes late. I open the door quietly and say sorry to the teacher. She smiles and tells me to sit down.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PEOPLE AND THE CELEBRATION
quests.situation: Today is your sister's birthday. Describe how your family celebrates at home.
quests.hint: Write about what people prepare and what they do together, then how your sister reacts.
quests.explanation: Celebrations are described by moving from preparation to the main moment to the reaction. Adding a feeling word, such as excited or surprised, gives the ending some emotion.
quests.modelAnswer: My mother bakes a chocolate cake in the morning, and our relatives arrive in the afternoon. We sing together while my sister blows out the candles. Then she opens her presents and looks very happy.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT THE CUSTOMER WANTS AND HOW YOU HELP
quests.situation: You work in a clothing store, and a customer wants a bigger size of a shirt. Describe what the customer asks and how you help.
quests.hint: Report what the customer says, describe your action, and say how the customer feels at the end.
quests.explanation: Service situations follow a request, an action and an outcome. Naming the three stages in that order makes even a short scene sound complete.
quests.modelAnswer: A customer asks me for a larger size of a blue shirt. I check the stockroom and find one on the bottom shelf. He tries it on, likes it, and pays at the counter.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE RIDE AND WHAT HAPPENS
quests.situation: You take a taxi from your hotel to the train station with your luggage. Describe the ride and how you pay at the end.
quests.hint: Follow the journey from the hotel door to the station and add one detail about the driver or the traffic.
quests.explanation: A short journey can be described in three parts: leaving, travelling and arriving. One detail about the driver or the traffic is enough; extra details make the sequence harder to read.
quests.modelAnswer: The hotel receptionist calls a taxi, and the driver puts my luggage in the trunk. The traffic is heavy, but we reach the station in twenty minutes. I pay the fare in cash and thank him.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT YOU NOTICE AND WHAT YOU DO
quests.situation: A new family moves into the apartment next to yours. Describe what you see in the hallway and what you do to welcome them.
quests.hint: Describe the scene first, then choose one friendly action and say how the new neighbors respond.
quests.explanation: Observation followed by action is a useful two-part structure: the first part shows what you notice and the second shows what you decide to do. The other person's reaction completes the exchange.
quests.modelAnswer: A moving truck stops in front of our building, and workers carry boxes up the stairs. In the hallway I meet a couple with two small children. I introduce myself and offer them a cold drink.

quests.instruction: WRITE ABOUT WHAT THE GROUP DOES
quests.situation: In your English class, the teacher asks you to make a poster in a group of three. Describe how the group works together.
quests.hint: Give each group member a different job and finish with what the group has at the end.
quests.explanation: Describing teamwork means giving actions to individuals rather than saying we did everything. Phrases like one student, another and I separate the roles clearly.
quests.modelAnswer: Our group has three students, and we share the work. One student suggests a title, another draws the pictures with markers, and I write the short text. In the end, we have a colorful poster.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS AND HOW PEOPLE REACT
quests.situation: The lights in your kitchen go out suddenly while your family is eating dinner. Describe what happens and how everyone reacts.
quests.hint: Show the change first, then describe two different reactions from two people.
quests.explanation: Reactions show the reader how important an event is. When different people react differently, for example one laughs and one acts, the scene feels more real.
quests.modelAnswer: Suddenly the kitchen becomes dark, and everyone stops eating. My little sister laughs, but my father gets up to find a flashlight. Soon we light a candle and finish dinner quietly.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT THE PEOPLE DO
quests.situation: It is noon at your workplace and the team takes a lunch break. Describe where people go and what they do.
quests.hint: Divide the team into two or three groups and say where each group eats.
quests.explanation: Grouping people is a good way to describe a crowd without listing every person. Phrases like some of them and others introduce each group and keep the sentences varied.
quests.modelAnswer: At noon, most of my colleagues stop working and go to the canteen. Some of them bring lunchboxes and heat their food in the microwave, while others buy hot meals. We talk about our plans for the weekend.

quests.instruction: TAP THE EMOJIS AND DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENS
quests.situation: You go to a shopping mall with a friend to buy new shoes. Describe what you see in the shop and what you decide.
quests.hint: Mention the shoes you look at, say why one pair is better, and finish with your decision.
quests.explanation: A decision is more convincing when a reason comes with it. Words such as but and so let you compare two options and lead the reader to your choice.
quests.modelAnswer: My friend and I walk through the mall to a large shoe shop. I try on two pairs of sneakers. The black ones look better, but the gray ones are cheaper and more comfortable, so I buy those.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE PEOPLE, PLACE, AND ACTIONS
quests.situation: You visit your grandparents' house on Saturday morning. Describe who is there, what you do together, and how the visit ends.
quests.hint: Plan a beginning, a middle and an ending before you write: arriving, spending time together, leaving.
quests.explanation: Even a short description benefits from a clear beginning, middle and end. A natural closing action, like leaving or saying goodbye, tells the reader the situation is complete.
quests.modelAnswer: We drive to my grandparents' house and arrive at ten. My grandmother welcomes us with a warm apple pie, and my grandfather shows me his garden. We eat together, and in the afternoon we say goodbye at the gate.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE THE SCENE AND HOW YOU FEEL
quests.situation: You are on a crowded train during rush hour on a Friday evening. Describe the people, the noise, and how you feel.
quests.hint: Choose one thing you see, one thing you hear, and one feeling, and connect them in a few sentences.
quests.explanation: A feeling is easier to believe when it follows from a detail. Saying the train is crowded and then that you feel tired explains the feeling instead of only announcing it.
quests.modelAnswer: The train is crowded, and I have to stand next to the door. Most passengers look at their phones, and a girl is listening to loud music. I feel tired, but I am happy because the weekend starts tomorrow.

quests.instruction: DESCRIBE WHAT YOU SEE ON THE WAY HOME
quests.situation: It is nine o'clock in the evening and you walk home through your neighborhood. Describe what you see and pass on the way.
quests.hint: Follow your walk from the first place you pass to your front door, adding one detail for each stop.
quests.explanation: A walk gives the description a natural order in space and time. Naming the places you pass, one after another, makes a neighborhood feel real without long sentences.
quests.modelAnswer: The streets are quiet, and the streetlights are already on. I pass the grocery shop while the owner closes the metal shutter. A gray cat crosses the road in front of me, and a few minutes later I reach my building.
